reason: The text demonstrates the opposite of this statement. Multiple elements contradict it: (1) Yahweh judges and condemns Ahab, a wicked leader, orchestrating his death in battle—not showing preferential care for leaders. (2) Micaiah explicitly describes Israel as scattered like sheep without a shepherd (וַיֹּ֤אמֶר רָאִ֤יתִי אֶת־ כָּל־ יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ נְפוֹצִ֣ים עַל־ הֶֽהָרִ֔ים כַּצֹּ֕אן אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֵין־ לָהֶ֖ם רֹעֶ֑ה), then Yahweh responds that they will return home in peace (לֹֽא־ אֲדֹנִ֣ים לָאֵ֔לֶּה יָשׁ֥וּבוּ אִישׁ־ לְבֵית֖וֹ בְּשָׁלֽוֹם)—showing clear empathy for the common people. (3) Jehoshaphat is rebuked for aiding the wicked king (הֲלָרָשָׁ֣ע לַעְזֹ֔ר וּלְשֹׂנְאֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה תֶּאֱהָ֑ב). (4) The extensive judicial reforms Jehoshaphat establishes are explicitly framed as serving the people's justice and welfare, with judges instructed to judge for Yahweh's justice (כִּ֣י לַיהוָ֑ה), emphasizing ethical governance.
